answer: A cosh blow from behind knocks an unaware man out for 10 to 30 s and counts as a strike. Death needs the finishing choice with a weapon or the rare fatal fall. Killing an officer brings a manhunt, 22 hours and a charge.
why: Nothing says what an unseen officer killing brings: arrest needs a witness or officer who saw. Whether a manhunt starts with no witness, and who is suspected, is not written.

answer: RT2-02 says an officer Frank strikes is a witness who knows it was him, so an arrest needs no statement. Knowing otherwise needs face to face, a fare, a naming or a face seen twice at 8 m.
why: Contradiction: RT2-02 makes any struck officer know Frank, yet a blow from behind shows no face and RT2-03 needs sight. Cosh from behind test only says it is seen as a strike.

answer: Nothing stops it: the old line against hitting Ellis or women officers was dropped on 24 Nov and no rule replaced it. Officer-struck rules would apply. Ellis is marked unable to die in her data, yet anyone can be killed.
why: Listed gaps: no replacement rule, no fallback for Ellis. police.json still holds the old never-lays-hands-on rule, and her record says can_die false against RT2-05. What happens to her case is unwritten.

answer: Allowed: Frank has no rule against striking a woman, and the strike input is never refused. RT2-02 says no rule replaces the old line about women officers (gap), so presumably the same officer-struck rules apply: 8 hours, a charge, Ellis up a stage.
why: The blueprint itself lists the woman-officer treatment as a gap. Same-as-any-officer is implied only, and police.json still carries the dropped never-strike rule.

answer: No. A knife wounds (hospital 5 game days, blood on Frank, 8 hours if arrested) and kills only by the finishing decision or the rare fatal fall. Fists never kill.
why: RT2-11 states it in one line and RT2-12 gives the fall conditions. Only how often the finishing choice is offered is unbounded (listed gap), which does not change the verb.

answer: Weapon out is rung 6 of the ladder, drawn on a held key, seen, and cannot be undrawn unseen. A threat said in talk is rung 3. Scatter and town reaction follow the draw. Drawing inside a talk scene is not stated.
why: No rule for drawing inside the talk camera or talk state, nor what the other man's reply does to it. Only the hold-up flow shows threatening again with a weapon out.

answer: No kick input exists. Finishing a downed man is a held strike for 2 s and 'Finish him?' asked twice. With fists it is a serious beating (hospital, days), with a weapon a killing. The story's 'put the boot in' conflicts.
why: Conflict C-341 is open: the frame wants a boot, the part has no kick. Until designed the part stands, so the player cannot do what the question asks.

answer: Weapons can be dropped down a drain; a bag thrown in the dock is gone but remembered by anyone who saw. Carried weapons are found in a search and must be got rid of. Tracing a found weapon to Frank is not covered.
why: Disposal is given, but nothing says a found weapon can or cannot be linked to him (no fingerprints rule; only research notes 1990 forensics compare and never name).

answer: Carried weapons (cosh, knuckleduster, knife, bat) come out on a held input, are seen, cannot be undrawn unseen; a swung improvised weapon takes 0.80 to 1.05 s to contact. No per-weapon list of draw, stab, put away and drop.
why: No move list per weapon: put away, drop and stab have no timings or inputs; damage order beyond bat more than cosh is a listed gap.

answer: 22 hours, then released without charge, on police bail pending inquiries, or charged and remanded. A charge joins Ellis's case and is read at the ending. There is no court scene and no prison for Frank.
why: Three exits are named with no rule choosing between them, and 'remanded' clashes with 'no prison'. The story's remand with visits is an open conflict.

answer: One bought detective constable loses one signed statement once for £200, from cash. He cannot go past a crime he saw. Nothing covers an exhibit, and nothing says a killing case is allowed.
why: Statements only; no exhibits exist as objects. Whether a murder statement counts, and what Ellis does when she notices the loss, is unwritten.

answer: Bought, Ellis still searches; her case cools twice as fast and she loses her best line once. Whether she still investigates a killing, and what the £100 a week buys her to do, is not ruled.
why: Listed gaps: what a bought Ellis does to her stages, RT-13 and a manhunt, and what the retainer buys. Her record still says cannot be bought.

answer: Killing an officer: a manhunt at once, 22 hours and a charge, losing the best turn of every ending. Fists cannot kill, so it needs a weapon or the fatal fall. The street's witnesses report; the killing never cools.
why: The aftermath is clear, but whether a witnessed killing may go straight to a manhunt is still open (C5), and how a constable fights or calls for help is not written.

answer: Yes. A fatal fall under the rare fall rule is treated as a killing, so an officer's death that way brings the same manhunt, 22 hours and charge. It is deterministic and needs a spent man at a kerb, step or wall.
why: The town treats the fall as a killing and the officer rule names the aftermath, so there is no murder or accident split to decide. A tester can replay the same fight.

answer: A hidden or sunk body is never found; the missing man becomes the town's question: landlady, mates and Ellis ask. The beat constable's place goes to the second constable from the next night.
why: Nothing says the station reacts to a missing officer (search, manhunt sign, Ellis stage) or who is suspected. Only generic missing-man asking is written.

answer: Go with him, or run: a chase. If lost, he is arrested when next met. Officer-seen deeds stay hot (hit-and-run 3 days, officer struck 7); a constable calls at the office at ten next morning at the soft edge. Running is not a crime.
why: Chase endings, search, hot spans and the next-meeting arrest are all given with numbers. Testable by seeded chases and golden rows.

answer: His hand on the collar means a search as if he stood; with cause (a weapon, the deed he saw) it is an arrest with that deed's hours. His next challenge is on cause, no talking round; seen again while hot, a new chase starts.
why: Explicit rule with the deed's hours and a new-chase trigger. Consistent across 2.6.2 and RT2-22.

answer: Nothing found. A grab holds a man about 2 s and a man put into railings is out for 4 s; no locking in rooms or yards, and no rule on the constable's absence or calling out.
why: Searched lock, shut in, trap, constable and door rules. No rule or input for confining a person.

answer: A threat is rung 3, an act with the seven slots, said in talk or shown. A threat can stop a witness's report to the police. Nothing says what a threat to an officer does.
why: Threat rules cover witnesses only. Whether threatening an officer is a crime he saw, loses him, or is shrugged off by his law trait is not written.

answer: A word talks him round if Frank has no cause. A search finds exactly what is carried, so a lie about the bag fails. Lies are acts with the seven slots. How a lie about his whereabouts is checked is not given.
why: Bag lies are moot, but no rule says how a constable tests a spoken alibi against what he knows, or what a caught lie costs.

answer: Only for a window: 2 hours and a caution if he owns up, against about 6 otherwise. No other deed has an owning-up row, and no input or talk line for owning up to a constable is written.
why: One offence only. For a wounding, robbery or killing nothing says whether owning up changes hours, charge or the case.

answer: Nothing found. A manhunt ends with an arrest or after three game days with no sighting; no way to hand himself in is written beyond walking up to an officer.
why: Searched surrender, give himself up, hand himself in, manhunt. No rule for ending a manhunt by going to the station.

answer: A lift from a pocket takes one thing worth taking (key, letter, wallet) from a person in a crowd. Whether a constable is a legal target, and his notebook, truncheon or radio as items, is not said.
why: Generic pickpocket rules only. No constable items, and the beat constable carries a truncheon only; a felt lift from an officer has no consequence written.

answer: The beat never changes by chance, so he can learn it; Mickey's door is in his sight at least every 4 minutes. A tail looks back every 20 to 40 s, a mark is a doubt. Nothing says the constable notices a follower.
why: Challenge causes (carrying, running, bloodied, where he should not be, weapon shown) omit following. The generic tail ladder is for job targets, not the beat.

answer: Officer-struck rules apply per officer (8 hours, a charge, Ellis up a stage). The second constable walks half a cycle behind only when the street is on edge. Hitting both at once, or killing one so the other fills the place, is not worked through.
why: No rule for two officers, stacking of charges or hours, or one calling for help. The killed beat man's place goes to the second constable only.

answer: The quay edge is one of the seven street places: a man put over it is in the water and climbs out at the nearest ladder within a minute. Whether that is an officer-struck deed with 8 hours is implied, not stated.
why: RT2-02 names striking and killing only, not shoving or dunking. Nothing says if an officer in the dock counts as struck, drowned, or just wet.

answer: Only his car can strike a person; a hit never kills. Under 10 mph a stagger, 10 to 25 knocked down, over 25 thrown down and moving within 20 s. Driving off is a hit-and-run: a chase, 8 hours and a charge.
why: Nothing says a hit on an officer counts as an officer struck (7 days hot, Ellis up) rather than a plain hit-and-run (3 days). Intent is not told apart.

answer: The patrol car is no faster than Frank's, stops on reckless acts, and a crash damages by closing speed. Nothing covers ramming it or running down its crew as an attack.
why: Crash damage and hit-and-run exist, but no rule on ramming a police car, a crew hurt or dead in it, or the aftermath. Cars never kill.

answer: The stop lasts under 2 minutes; striking an officer is arrested when next met, 8 hours and a charge, Ellis up, the manhunt sign if he knocks one out and gets away. Two crew in the car is not worked through.
why: Officer-struck rule covers one man; no rule for a driver and passenger together, the radio, or reinforcements when a crew is attacked.

answer: Yes, with a gun that has reached him. Before War a hit wounds and never kills. At Fired armed officers come slowly; Ellis goes up a step. Struck-officer rules (8 hours, a charge) presumably apply to a wounded one.
why: The wound-only rule is explicit and tested by dial states. Only the extra hours for a shot officer are implied, a minor gap.

answer: At War a body hit can kill, a named permanent event. Killing an officer: a manhunt at once, 22 hours and a charge, best turn of every ending lost. Armed cars work the streets and stop and search at two fixed points; Ellis goes up.
why: The kill, the manhunt, hours and charge, and the armed response are all given. Armed car numbers and timings are a listed gap but the verb and result are clear.

answer: Not covered. Hold-ups are only for shops and named adults with a till or purse. A weapon out at an officer is rung 6 of the ladder, an act the town sees; armed response starts only at Fired.
why: No rule for pointing a gun at an officer: his reaction, what he hands over, or the charge. The hold-up chain lists no officer as a target.

answer: An honest officer offered a note makes it a crime he saw: an arrest with cause. Only the two bought men take a note, once each. What happens on an offer the second time is not written.
why: First offer is clear (arrest with cause). A second offer, or a bribe to Garton after his one use, has no stated outcome. The offer's hours are not named.

answer: A hook is a fact Frank holds about a person; spending it buys a recruit, an answer or a counter, once. Nothing makes constables hook targets. Wardell owes money in town, Garton fears Ellis, but no rule uses them.
why: Hooks are written for rivals and crew. Police blackmail has no price, outcome or limit, and a bluff 'works only if believed' without a belief rule.

answer: Each bought man acts once and no more. Past his limit is a crime he saw. The old prototype allowed 99 uses and is overruled. Whether leaning on him by threat or hook gets a second favour is not written.
why: Paid favour is clear; 'paid or leaned on' is said but leaning has no rule, price or limit, and a second payment for a second favour is not addressed.

answer: Nothing specific. An officer remembers like anyone and a colleague who sees a payment keeps it. Wardell's temper has mouth 0.7 and sells facts to Danny. No rule says what a questioned bought officer says.
why: Only general memory and temper exist. No event for a bought officer under question, no limit to what he gives, and Ellis noticing is only noted on the card.

answer: No. A bought officer Frank strikes stops being bought for good, and a struck officer is a witness who knows it was him, so nobody needs to have seen.
why: Flat rule, no seen condition, and the knowing comes with the strike. Contradiction only for a blow from behind (Q002), not for a face-to-face blow.

answer: Killing any officer is a manhunt at once, 22 hours and a charge, and a body found brings Ellis. The bought man's use is lost. No fallback for Garton's or Wardell's role is written.
why: Aftermath of killing an officer is clear, but killing a bought man to stop talk is not told apart, and RT2-05 gives no fallback for Garton or Wardell.

answer: Talk alone never makes an arrest; an arrest needs a signed statement from someone who knew the man or an officer who saw. An anonymous 999 call brings a constable but never an arrest alone. Framing a named rival is not covered.
why: The tip rule is said to be under 3.1.2 but is not there. Whether Frank's own word or a call can name a rival, and its effect, is not written.

answer: Nothing found. Searched plant, frame, evidence, rival's lock-up. Evidence exists only as what a search finds on a person; no planting verb.
why: No input or rule to leave goods or a weapon on a rival or in a lock-up, or for a search of one.

answer: A phone box call is 10p; 999 is free; an anonymous call brings a constable to the spot that night but never makes an arrest alone. A gun call at Fired brings armed officers. A tip about a place where nothing happened is not covered.
why: Calls are written for a deed at a spot. A lock-up search on a tip, the rival's response and the case effect are not written.

answer: Not written. The station is not placed on the plan and has no interior (a listed gap); it is used for custody, and Ellis's desk is there from 08:30 on weekdays.
why: The station is only the place custody happens. Nothing says Frank may walk in, who is at the desk, or what he can do there.

answer: Giving Ellis a rival removes one charge from the case, and 'nobody given to Ellis' is a condition of the best ending turn. What it costs on the street is not stated.
why: The gain is given, the cost is not: who learns, how the telling spreads, and the rival's reply are unwritten.

answer: Nothing. Custody is skipped time under 2 minutes: the station, the duty solicitor, the hours pass. No interview scene is played, so silence has no outcome.
why: Searched interview, silence, no comment, question. No interview exists, so nothing differs by what he says.

answer: The duty solicitor is free and always there. A solicitor's brief costs about £50 a week and the story wants 'a cheaper way (a brief at a fee)', but what a paid one does beyond the duty man is not written.
why: Price exists, effect does not: no hours cut, no charge dropped, no statement beaten. Listed as partly covered.

answer: Found on him in a search, the envelope or a weapon gives an arrest, and what he carries is kept. A gun at a War stop is 12 hours, a charge and the gun kept. Hours for the envelope and its fate are not stated.
why: No hours for carrying the envelope, nothing says what the outfit does when it is kept, and Ron's debt rule covers only a robbed envelope.

answer: Custody hours pass as skipped time and the street sees him go. Nothing says what the crew do, whether appointments or jobs fail, or if rank slips. No lateness fail inside a window of two game hours.
why: Only the time cost is written. A 22-hour hold across a night job or an appointment has no rule, and Ron's later custody is a listed gap.

answer: Never taken twice for one deed. Charges accumulate one per arrest that ends in a charge. Two deeds at once: the hours (sum, longest, or one case adding 2) are not decided.
why: The same-deed half is clear. Two deeds in one arrest has no hours rule and the case merge figure applies only to street crimes and the fire.

answer: No prison, no court scene, no trial. An arrest ends in a caution or a charge and bail; the charge joins Ellis's case and is read at the ending. The story's remand hearings are an open conflict for Ron.
why: Clear for Frank and consistent with canon's no-prison line. Only the remanded wording in 2.6.4 and the story's Ron remand clash, noted as gaps.

answer: Nothing found. A charge means bail into Act III; no conditions, no reporting, no penalty for leaving. Driving out of the Hook just comes back as time passed.
why: Searched bail, skip, leave town, conditions. Bail has no terms, so skipping it is unaddressed.

answer: A chase reaching the soft edge ends as lost: the pursuer turns back, Frank is out 30 game minutes and returns, and the patrol waits on the edge road all night. A manhunt is not a chase; whether leaving ends it is not said.
why: Edge rule is for chases and night patrol. Nothing says a manhunt (Ellis stage 4) pauses, cools or is escaped by leaving; only three days unseen ends it.

answer: Ellis's stages show signs first: a car on the street and his description said aloud at stage four; a manhunt falls after three days unseen. Door knocking next morning, one office search with notice and War stops are separate. No minute by minute.
why: No manhunt routine: no roadblocks (only fixed War stops), no door-to-door plan beyond the knock rule, and an office search is tied to investigating, not manhunt.

answer: A reload gives the same next hour; the game autosaves after every deed and holds a save during a fight. Memory of people is kept. The state of a live chase or manhunt stage is not named as saved.
why: Saving is covered, but the pursuit, search timers and Ellis's stage are not listed as saved, and saving mid chase has no rule.

answer: Yes, by game days: Ellis falls a stage after two quiet weeks, a manhunt to investigating after three days unseen, hot deeds cool in 3 to 7 days; a killing never cools. A sleep or wait stops for a constable at the door.
why: Cooling is by game clock, so skipping and sleeping count; the exceptions (killing never cools, dial never to 0) are stated and testable.

answer: A chase is lost once the constable has not seen him for 7 s or the gap is over 70 m unseen; yards, ginnels and six vaults help. Entering buildings mid chase, and the constable following in, is not said.
why: Hiding on foot is by sight breaking only; buildings, locked doors and an officer entering one are not written, and the 80 m search stops short of them.

answer: A coat change sheds a slot only against witnesses who have not yet told; the coat buys doubt about the face, none about the car. An officer who knows him sees through it at 25 m; a description needs two marks.
why: Rules are there, but no time or place for a change mid chase, and no check that a pursuer who watches him swap still follows.

answer: A second car sheds a slot against witnesses who have not told; a parked car takes about 6 s by force and is loud. A car chase is lost after 7 s unseen or a gap over 200 m. A noted plate stays for good.
why: No mid-chase rule: a pursuer who sees the swap, the owner reporting the theft and the stolen car's plate are not tied together.

answer: Respray or new plates clear a noted plate only for witnesses who have not yet told anyone; the station keeps every plate noted and a noted plate is known for good. No cost, time or supplier for plates.
why: Listed gap: no price, time or place for plates (only Hewson's paint). The police half reads as not cleared, which the player is not told.

answer: He challenges on suspicion: carrying at night, running, bloodied, where he should not be, or a weapon shown. By day he walks Quay Street and the north road to the cold-store road. The causes are not split by day and night.
why: Day challenges are implied: only 'carrying at night' is time bound and a day-only list is missing, with no day cause for what Frank carries.

answer: A body is dragged at 0.9 m/s, boot in 4 s, or into the dock in 3 s; a seen move is an act with seven slots a witness tells. 'Carrying at night' and 'bloodied' are challenge causes. No body-seen rule is written.
why: What a constable or a witness does on seeing a body carried is not written by itself: no flee-or-tell rule, no instant arrest, no day case.

answer: Ellis is at her desk 08:30 to 18:30 weekdays and goes to a home point outside the Hook at the north edge. A tail looks back every 20 to 40 s and a mark is a doubt. Her home is not walkable.
why: Her home is only a schedule point beyond the edge, with no map, route or noticing rule for her (nerve 0.9). Whether she makes a tail is not written.

answer: Not written. The station has no plan position or interior (listed gap) and Ellis's home is only an off-map point. Break-in rules exist for ordinary places.
why: Searched break in, station, home. No rule says either is enterable, or what a break-in at police premises brings.

answer: A threat is rung 3, an act with the seven slots. The old line against touching Ellis is dropped. Her card says she never threatens; her temper is level. What a threat to her does is not written.
why: No rule for threatening a detective: her reply, a crime she saw, or a stage change. police.json still bars striking her, against the 24 Nov ruling.

answer: Nothing found. Hooks are facts about a person spent once; being bought is something she remembers. No rule makes the bribe a hook against her, and her record still says she cannot be bought.
why: Searched blackmail, hook, Ellis. No hook source, price or outcome for leverage over a bought officer.

answer: A missed week ends it for good: her case jumps 3 points, she remembers, and she is never bought twice. Pay day is every seventh game day, paid from cash only. It cannot be bought again.
why: Explicit and numbered across the part, the data and the economy design. Testable by a seeded missed week.

answer: Lies are acts with the seven slots; talk alone brings questions, never an arrest; a bluff works only if believed. Ellis knows what she was told and 'reads the line back'. How she tests a lie is not written.
why: No rule for her checking a statement against her facts, or the cost of a caught lie. Claim check covers what characters say, not what they believe.

answer: Not written for Ellis in general. Owning up cuts a window's custody to 2 hours with a caution. In week 5 Frank may sign for Ron's blame himself, which is a story beat, not a talk option.
why: Only the window deed has an owning-up rule, and nothing says what owning up to a detective in talk does to her case or stage.

answer: Nothing found. She comes down Quay Street for talk from day 2 once three of his day people pass on talk; her card says level, never jokes on duty. Friendship is written only for Alison and Danby.
why: Searched flirt, befriend, regard. No rule lets Ellis become a friend or reacts to flirting; her regard sits at 0.2 with no ladder.

answer: Her data says she cannot die; RT2-05 says anyone can be killed and the story falls back by role, but no fallback for Ellis is written. The fire thread runs on through Alison and Ellis.
why: Listed gap: no role fallback for Ellis, and her record contradicts 'anyone can be killed'. Who carries her case and stages is not written.

answer: She can be bought for about £800 cash once, week 6 in the economy run, by an authored scene. An honest officer offered a note is a crime he saw. Whether an early or short offer is arrested or refused is not written.
why: The ruled time and the early or no money response are missing; data says authored scene, part says bribe, and the honest-officer rule would arrest.
